newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Key players take stage in Belgian Rwanda inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Key players take stage in Belgian Rwanda inquiry.

text.p: The three principal players in Belgium's decision to send troops to Rwanda in 1993 took the stage before a senate inquiry on Wednesday swearing they had no inkling of the genocide that was to erupt a few months later.

Belgium sent 350 troops to join the United Nations force in Rwanda in November 1993, 10 of whom were hacked to death on April 7 -- the day after the plane carrying Hutu President Juvenal Habyarimana was shot down and the genocide began.

The Belgian government has come under increasing criticism that it misread and mishandled the situation, particularly the growing resentment against the former colonial power seen by many radical Hutus as having sold them down the river.
"You cannot talk of a general anti-Belgian climate," Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told the five-member senate commission investigating the events leading up to the deaths.
The inquiry is sensitive because it involves a serving prime minister.
Former NATO seretary general Willy Claes, who was Belgian foreign minister at the time, repeatedly said there was no indication of a pervasive anti-Belgian mood in Rwanda.
"It was well known that there were armed bands and arms caches...but I don't think you can talk of a broad anti-Belgian feeling," he said.
He pointed out that Belgium was the biggest donor of foreign aid to the country and had close relations with Habyarimana who had for months been fighting a civil war with invading Tutsis.
"It was an ideal peacekeeping situation, both parties had agreed," Claes told the senators, citing the Hutu-Tutsi power-sharing deal signed in the Tanzanian capital Arusha.
Leo Delcroix, defence minister at the time, said hindsight was all very well, but there had certainly been no crisis when the decision was made to include Belgian troops in the U.N. contingent.

However, in the years since the mass slaughter of Tutsis following the killing of Habyarimana, information has come to light suggesting that Belgium and the United Nations Security Council had ample evidence of the looming humanitarian disaster.

Senator Alain Destexhe, a worker in Rwanda for Medecins Sans Frontiers at the time, has published two books on the genocide -- one of which includes a telex sent to New York in January 1994 by U.N. Commander Romeo Dallaire.

This telex sets out in detail information from a top member of the Rwandan government who states that the growing demonstrations against opposition politicians were being organised to incite the Belgians to open fire and give the militants the excuse they needed.
It also gives details of the numbers and intentions of the groups of militant Hutu Interahamwe militia scattered in and around the Rwandan capital Kigali -- where the genocide started.
For Destexhe, a member of the senate commission, it is not a matter of some kind of government plot but more a question of a combination of incompetence and naivety.
He notes that at the same time as Belgium had troops among the neutral U.N. forces it still had 23 military advisers working for the Rwandan government.
The commission is due to publish its report at the end of July.
